name: Kohata no O Sugi (Kohata's Great Cedar)

location.address: Kohata, Haruja 49-2 (also written 治家49-2), Nihonmatsu City, Fukushima Prefecture, within the grounds of Okitsushima Shrine (隠津島神社), on Mt Kohata, beside the subsidiary Kado Shrine (門神社)

access: Free, shrine grounds. Reached via the shrine's main approach (omote-sando) off route 117, a stone stairway from the first torii up Mt Kohata; parking (~10 cars) near the approach entrance and ~5 more near the second shrine office. This is a genuine climb, not a flat stroll, but no permission or ticket is needed.
transport: About 20 min by car from Adachi Station, 25 min from Matsukawa Station, 35 min from Nihonmatsu Station (all JR Tohoku Main Line); no direct public transit to the shrine.
verify_notes: REAL PLACE: Nihonmatsu City, not Miharu (Otama and Nihonmatsu are both in the same general Fukushima area as Miharu but are three distinct municipalities; roughly 20-24km from central Miharu, so likely not the same walkable page unless treated as a wider day-trip area). National Natural Monument since 27 March 1941 (Showa 16). Stands in the precinct of Okitsushima Shrine, an old shrine (founded per legend in 769 CE, dedicated to the three Munakata goddesses, historically called Benzaiten-gu and still known locally as 'Kohata's Benten-sama'), specifically on the north side of its subsidiary Kado Shrine building. Ranked as the 10th-largest tree in Fukushima Prefecture. FLAG on measurements: city's own page gives height 20m and trunk girth 9.33m (at breast height); ja.Wikipedia cites a 2016-17 Fukushima Prefecture Forest Planning Division survey giving height 29.0m and trunk girth 9.9m at 1.3m height. Root girth 16.2m recorded in a 1940 survey (both sources agree on this figure). Recorded girth_cm as 933 (the more conservative, city-sourced figure); note the prefecture's 990cm alternative in case the writer wants the higher figure. Age given as 780 years (Wikipedia, tied to the prefecture survey) or approx 800 years (city page); used range 780-800. FLAG on vitality: lightning strike damage has hollowed the main trunk; the cavity has been sealed (resin/copper plate per different sources) and the tree is held up by more than ten support struts to prevent toppling. It is alive and actively maintained/braced, not dead, but should be described honestly as a veteran under active support rather than a pristine giant. Photographed 25 Oct 2023 (same photographer and same day as Baba Zakura, tmpa_001, suggesting a single Fukushima giant-tree touring day), geotagged to 37°37'18.99"N 140°34'33.36"E which converts to the exact coordinates given in the lead, confirming tree-level precision. The shrine grounds are also home to other large cedars and cypresses reportedly planted by daimyo Gamo Ujisato, in case a second tree at the same site is worth a future lead.

name: Sugisawa no O Sugi (Sugisawa's Great Cedar)
age_estimate: roughly 1,000 years (city and prefecture both use this figure; one source gives a wider possible range)

location.address: Sugisawa, Taira 97 (also written Sugisawa-aza-Taira 97), Nihonmatsu City, Fukushima Prefecture

access: Free, public land (managed by the Sugisawa administrative district on national land). Bus: from Nihonmatsu Station take the Sugisawa bus to the 'Sugisawa Taigi' stop, then 5 min on foot. Car: about 30 min from Nihonmatsu Station or 35 min from Nihonmatsu IC (Tohoku Expressway).
transport: Bus from Nihonmatsu Station (JR Tohoku Main Line) to Sugisawa Taigi stop, then a 5-minute walk.
verify_notes: REAL PLACE: Nihonmatsu City (Iwashiro area), not Miharu; a different tree and a different part of Nihonmatsu from Kohata no O Sugi (tmpa_002), several km apart. National Natural Monument since 24 August 1943, also a Fukushima Prefectural Green Cultural Property since 1983. Local legend: in 1643 the Nihonmatsu domain lord Niwa Mitsushige rested under the tree during an inspection tour, was so struck by it that he renamed the village 'Sugisawa' after it. Genuinely healthy: ja.Wikipedia describes it as having 'vigorous vitality' with minimal trunk decay for its age, and records active conservation work: cavity treatment, root reinforcement and support installation in 1986-87, and root-soil improvement plus anti-trampling measures for visitors in 2006-08. This is the strongest-vitality candidate of the four leads. FLAG on measurements, sources disagree more than usual: city page gives height 50m, trunk girth 12.8m (measurement height unstated); Wikipedia gives height 50-68m, root girth 22.5m, and breast-height girth 10.9m, noting the trunk divides into 5 main stems from 6.6m up, spreading 25-30m across, which likely explains why different sources report different 'girth' figures depending on whether they measured the single base or something else. Recorded girth_cm as 1090 (the standard breast-height measurement from Wikipedia); the city's 1280cm figure and the 2250cm root girth are noted here for the writer. The 68m upper height figure is unusually tall for a sugi and worth treating cautiously; used age_max 1000 per both sources but kept age_min lower (600) to reflect Wikipedia's stated range. Photographed by the same photographer (Sakaori) as tmpa_001 and tmpa_002, license CC BY 4.0 (not BY-SA like tmpa_002, check licence per photo), geotagged to 37°30'38.24"N 140°34'45.88"E which converts to the exact lead coordinates, confirming tree-level precision.
